edg5000 · Nov 28, 2026

Generally, asking it to review will almost always find real issues without overblown severity. The key is that once the model ends the turn after delivering on a task, it won't do this audit by itself, but how you prompt it won't matter much, as long as you let it evaluate the work as an explicit task. I call these "audits" and do this constantly. This can be either a new session or the existing one, does not matter that much for the results, although I generally use clean sessions for this. One risk is them reading each others' scratch dirs, which can make the audit no longer fully independent.

loufe · Nov 28, 2026

Yeah, the "review" cycle usually lasts a few turns, for me, too.

1. Ask for a precommit review, with a structured list of usual issues. Simultaneously, deploy a "you're responsible for the maintenance of this codebase" review agent, an adversarial review agent, and another agent.

2. Review the agents' findings, triage, confirm what's actually an issue. What is the issue, what are our options, what's modern best practice, what is the codebase precedent, what do our rules and ADR files say, what are the trade-offs, what do you suggest and why?

3. Manual review, pushback. Deploy another agent or two to review the potential issues and the suggested fix(es), especially if I feel a bit out my depth. Try doing "audits" in scratches, similar to what you do, it seems, where necessary.

4. Implement. Possibly return to a more limited step 1 if necessary.

I have the disadvantage of no formal programming training, but I do quite enjoy digging into architecture design and good and bad patterns and abstractions. It's working for me well so far, over a year into production of my work project. Fortunately I found my intuition about the data and DB modeling has been good, so it's been easy to expand things in that way.

Model capabilities have also grown as the complexity of that project has also grown, which has made keeping a linear velocity possible. It's very rewarding being able to allot as much time as I do to refactoring and cleaning up the codebase with time - I'm sure not everyone has that. It's probably the only thing keeping the project from feeling like slop.
